choices.text: Depends on the mass of the substance

questions.explanation: A mole is a counting word like a dozen: one mole always means 6.02 × 10²³ particles, no matter which substance it is. It is the mass of those particles that changes, not the count.
questions.prompt: How many particles are there in one mole of any substance?

questions.answer: n = m / M = 12 g / 12 g/mol = 1 mol. Weighing 12 g of carbon gives exactly one mole.
questions.explanation: Use n = m / M with m = 12 g and M = 12 g/mol for carbon-12: 12 / 12 = 1 mol. The scale has counted 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms for you.
questions.prompt: Calculate the number of moles in 12 g of carbon-12. (Molar mass of carbon-12 = 12 g/mol) Show your working with n = m / M.

questions.answer: 2 mol of oxygen, making 4 mol of water. The ratio in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O is 2 : 1 : 2, so doubling the hydrogen from 2 mol to 4 mol doubles the oxygen from 1 mol to 2 mol and the water from 2 mol to 4 mol.
questions.explanation: Balanced equations give mole ratios, not mass ratios: read the 2 : 1 : 2 ratio off the equation and scale the whole ratio by the same factor.
questions.prompt: For the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of oxygen are needed to react with 4 mol of hydrogen, and how many moles of water are made? Explain using the mole ratio.

title: The mole: counting atoms by weighing
